title: Curiosity Is How Long You Stay in Discovery Mode
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that curiosity is less about asking questions and more about how long a person is willing to stay engaged in an inquiry once it becomes uncomfortable. The author frames conversational curiosity as a discipline built around a single repeatable question -- 'What makes you say that?' -- deployed without agenda or judgment to peel back layers of reasoning. A worked dialogue example shows how successive rounds of the question move a colleague from a surface complaint to a deeper, more honest admission. The piece closes by reframing curiosity as an orientation of humility rather than a technique to master.
points: Curiosity is defined as staying power in an inquiry, not just the willingness to ask questions.
A single repeatable prompt -- 'What makes you say that?' -- works because it makes no assumptions and suspends judgment.
The worked A/B dialogue demonstrates how successive layers of the same question can surface a person's real, underlying belief.
Judgment closes conversations; curiosity keeps them open, which is why the two states can't coexist.
quotes: It’s more about how long people stay engaged in the inquiry. Curious people stay engaged longer, even when it’s uncomfortable.
Thinking of conversations as layers is the ideal metaphor for becoming more curious.
The question set works to promote curiosity because of what it doesn’t do. It makes no assumptions about the answer, and it suspends any judgment.
Curiosity isn’t a technique. It’s the discipline of arriving empty and staying longer in discovery mode.
People are never curious and certain at the same time. If you agree, our curiosity demands we explore why you do.
